# The taxonomy, in full

An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
causes.

This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
cause's card.

Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
`step.py done 1`.

## Categories

| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |

## Every root cause, one line each

### C1 — Redundant Computation

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |

### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |

### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |

### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |

### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |

### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |

### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |

### C8 — Missing Reuse

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |

### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |

### C10 — Underused Language Primitives

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |

### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |

### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |

## Using this well

**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.

**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
card is the claim.

**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.

**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
either attribution is fine — say which you chose.

## What tools can and cannot contribute

Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody

  part of the job.
- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.

Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.

1	# The taxonomy, in full
2	
3	An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
4	need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
5	program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
6	causes.
7	
8	This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
9	keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
10	there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
11	**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
12	recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
13	cause's card.
14	
15	Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
16	the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
17	`step.py done 1`.
18	
19	## Categories
20	
21	| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
24	| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
25	| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
26	| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
27	| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
28	| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
29	| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
30	| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
31	| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
32	| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
33	| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
34	| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |
35	
36	## Every root cause, one line each
37	
38	### C1 — Redundant Computation
39	
40	| ID | Name | Looks for |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
43	| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
44	| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
45	| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
46	| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
47	| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
48	| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
49	| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |
50	
51	### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead
52	
53	| ID | Name | Looks for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
56	| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
57	| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |
58	
59	### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns
60	
61	| ID | Name | Looks for |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
64	| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
65	| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
66	| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
67	| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
68	| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
69	| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |
70	
71	### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow
72	
73	| ID | Name | Looks for |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
76	| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
77	| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
78	| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
79	| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
80	| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
81	| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
82	| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |
83	
84	### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures
85	
86	| ID | Name | Looks for |
87	|---|---|---|
88	| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
89	| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
90	| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
91	| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |
92	
93	### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage
94	
95	| ID | Name | Looks for |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
98	| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
99	| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
100	| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
101	| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
102	| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
103	| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |
104	
105	### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic
106	
107	| ID | Name | Looks for |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
110	| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
111	| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
112	| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
113	| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |
114	
115	### C8 — Missing Reuse
116	
117	| ID | Name | Looks for |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
120	| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
121	| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
122	| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |
123	
124	### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access
125	
126	| ID | Name | Looks for |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
129	| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
130	| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
131	| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |
132	
133	### C10 — Underused Language Primitives
134	
135	| ID | Name | Looks for |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
138	| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
139	| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
140	| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
141	| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
142	| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |
143	
144	### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management
145	
146	| ID | Name | Looks for |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
149	| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
150	| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
151	| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
152	| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |
153	
154	### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage
155	
156	| ID | Name | Looks for |
157	|---|---|---|
158	| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
159	| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
160	| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
161	| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |
162	
163	## Using this well

165	**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a

168	**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three

1	# The taxonomy, in full
2	
3	An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
4	need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
5	program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
6	causes.
7	
8	This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
9	keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
10	there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
11	**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
12	recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
13	cause's card.
14	
15	Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
16	the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
17	`step.py done 1`.
18	
19	## Categories
20	
21	| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
24	| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
25	| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
26	| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
27	| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
28	| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
29	| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
30	| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
31	| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
32	| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
33	| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
34	| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |
35	
36	## Every root cause, one line each
37	
38	### C1 — Redundant Computation
39	
40	| ID | Name | Looks for |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
43	| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
44	| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
45	| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
46	| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
47	| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
48	| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
49	| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |
50	
51	### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead
52	
53	| ID | Name | Looks for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
56	| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
57	| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |
58	
59	### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns
60	
61	| ID | Name | Looks for |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
64	| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
65	| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
66	| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
67	| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
68	| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
69	| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |
70	
71	### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow
72	
73	| ID | Name | Looks for |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
76	| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
77	| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
78	| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
79	| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
80	| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
81	| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
82	| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |
83	
84	### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures
85	
86	| ID | Name | Looks for |
87	|---|---|---|
88	| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
89	| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
90	| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
91	| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |
92	
93	### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage
94	
95	| ID | Name | Looks for |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
98	| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
99	| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
100	| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
101	| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
102	| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
103	| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |
104	
105	### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic
106	
107	| ID | Name | Looks for |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
110	| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
111	| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
112	| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
113	| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |
114	
115	### C8 — Missing Reuse
116	
117	| ID | Name | Looks for |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
120	| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
121	| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
122	| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |
123	
124	### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access
125	
126	| ID | Name | Looks for |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
129	| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
130	| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
131	| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |
132	
133	### C10 — Underused Language Primitives
134	
135	| ID | Name | Looks for |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
138	| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
139	| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
140	| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
141	| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
142	| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |
143	
144	### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management
145	
146	| ID | Name | Looks for |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
149	| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
150	| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
151	| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
152	| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |
153	
154	### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage
155	
156	| ID | Name | Looks for |
157	|---|---|---|
158	| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
159	| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
160	| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
161	| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |
162	
163	## Using this well
164	
165	**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
166	category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.
167	
168	**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
169	or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
170	than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
171	enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
172	card is the claim.
173	
174	**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
175	on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
176	like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.
177	
178	**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
179	either attribution is fine — say which you chose.
180	
181	## What tools can and cannot contribute
182	
183	Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody
184	described in advance. That makes rules dependable about the shapes they know
185	and completely blind to everything else. Two consequences, and they point in
186	opposite directions:
187	
188	- **A rule firing has observed a pattern, not diagnosed a problem.** Every
189	  pattern in this taxonomy is the right thing to write somewhere, which is what
190	  each card's `Looks like it, but is not` section records.
191	  Some of what any rule reports is therefore wrong here, and saying which is
192	  part of the job.
193	- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
194	  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
195	  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
196	  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.
197	
198	Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
199	second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.
200

25	def read_impressions_file(file_name, click_map):
26	    if not os.path.exists(file_name):
27	        print("{} not found.".format(file_name))
28	        sys.exit(1)
29	    print("Reading impressions data from " + file_name)
30	
31	    with io.open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
32	        field_list = ["id", "user_id", "timestamp", "history", "impressions"]
33	        reader = csv.DictReader(f, delimiter="\t", fieldnames=field_list)
34	        for line in reader:
35	            for impression in line["impressions"].split(" "):
36	                news_id, label = impression.split("-")
37	                click_map[news_id]["impressions"] += 1
38	                if label == "1":
39	                    click_map[news_id]["clicks"] += 1
40	
41	
42	def convert_file(output, file_name, docids, click_map):
43	    if not os.path.exists(file_name):
44	        print("{} not found.".format(file_name))
45	        sys.exit(1)
46	    print("Reading news data from " + file_name)
47	
48	    with io.open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
49	
50	        field_list = ["news_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract", "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"]
51	        include_fields = set(field_list[0:6])
52	
53	        reader = csv.DictReader(f, delimiter="\t", fieldnames=field_list)
54	        for line in reader:
55	            if line["news_id"] in docids:
56	                continue
57	            if len(docids) > 0:
58	                output.write(",\n")
59	            docid = line["news_id"]
60	            docids.add(docid)
61	
62	            clicks = click_map[docid]["clicks"]
63	            impressions = click_map[docid]["impressions"]
64	
65	            doc = {"put": f"id:{doc_type}:{doc_type}::{docid}", "fields" : {} }
66	            for field in include_fields:
67	                doc["fields"][field] = line[field]
68	            doc["fields"]["date"] = generate_random_date()  # data set does not include a publish date
69	            doc["fields"]["clicks"] = clicks
70	            doc["fields"]["impressions"] = impressions
71	            json.dump(doc, output)

23	field_list = ["docid", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract", "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"]
24	
25	
26	def create_embeddings(input_file_name, output_file_name):
27	    docids = set()
28	    titles = {}
29	    abstracts = {}
30	    categories = {}
31	    subcategories = {}
32	
33	    # read
34	    with io.open(input_file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
35	        reader = csv.DictReader(f, delimiter="\t", fieldnames=field_list)

49	    t = time.time()
50	    with open(output_file_name, "w") as f:
51	        for i, docid in enumerate(docids):
52	            title = titles[docid]

54	
55	            f.write(docid)

57	            tokens = tokenizer(title, abstract, return_tensors="pt", max_length=100, truncation=True, padding=True)

63	            if i % (len(docids)//100) == (len(docids)//100 - 1):
64	                print("Completed {} embeddings ({:.0f} %) [{:.2f} s]".format(i + 1, 100.0 *(i+1)/len(docids), time.time()-t))
65	                t = time.time()

67	
68	def write_embedding(f, embedding):
69	    f.write("\t")
70	    for j, num in enumerate(embedding):
71	        if j > 0:
72	            f.write(",")
73	        f.write("%.4f" % num)
74	
75	
76	def main():
77	    create_embeddings(train_news_file, train_embedding_file)

# The taxonomy, in full

An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
causes.

This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
cause's card.

Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
`step.py done 1`.

## Categories

| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |

## Every root cause, one line each

### C1 — Redundant Computation

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |

### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |

### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |

### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |

### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |

### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |

### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |

### C8 — Missing Reuse

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |

### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |

### C10 — Underused Language Primitives

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |

### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |

### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage

| ID | Name | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |

## Using this well

**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.

**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
card is the claim.

**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.

**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
either attribution is fine — say which you chose.

## What tools can and cannot contribute

Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody
described in advance. That makes rules dependable about the shapes they know
and completely blind to everything else. Two consequences, and they point in
opposite directions:

- **A rule firing has observed a pattern, not diagnosed a problem.** Every
  pattern in this taxonomy is the right thing to write somewhere, which is what
  each card's `Looks like it, but is not` section records.
  Some of what any rule reports is therefore wrong here, and saying which is
  part of the job.
- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.

Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.

63	                                   - Rule 4: You may get an empty resultset as an answer. In this case, apologize and ask the the user if they are looking for something else.

content.content:
1	# The taxonomy, in full
2	
3	An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
4	need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
5	program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
6	causes.
7	
8	This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
9	keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
10	there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
11	**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
12	recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
13	cause's card.
14	
15	Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
16	the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
17	`step.py done 1`.
18	
19	## Categories
20	
21	| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
24	| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
25	| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
26	| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
27	| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
28	| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
29	| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
30	| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
31	| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
32	| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
33	| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
34	| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |
35	
36	## Every root cause, one line each
37	
38	### C1 — Redundant Computation
39	
40	| ID | Name | Looks for |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
43	| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
44	| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
45	| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
46	| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
47	| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
48	| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
49	| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |
50	
51	### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead
52	
53	| ID | Name | Looks for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
56	| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
57	| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |
58	
59	### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns
60	
61	| ID | Name | Looks for |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
64	| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
65	| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
66	| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
67	| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
68	| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
69	| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |
70	
71	### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow
72	
73	| ID | Name | Looks for |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
76	| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
77	| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
78	| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
79	| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
80	| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
81	| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
82	| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |
83	
84	### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures
85	
86	| ID | Name | Looks for |
87	|---|---|---|
88	| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
89	| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
90	| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
91	| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |
92	
93	### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage
94	
95	| ID | Name | Looks for |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
98	| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
99	| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
100	| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
101	| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
102	| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
103	| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |
104	
105	### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic
106	
107	| ID | Name | Looks for |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
110	| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
111	| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
112	| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
113	| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |
114	
115	### C8 — Missing Reuse
116	
117	| ID | Name | Looks for |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
120	| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
121	| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
122	| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |
123	
124	### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access
125	
126	| ID | Name | Looks for |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
129	| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
130	| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
131	| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |
132	
133	### C10 — Underused Language Primitives
134	
135	| ID | Name | Looks for |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
138	| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
139	| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
140	| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
141	| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
142	| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |
143	
144	### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management
145	
146	| ID | Name | Looks for |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
149	| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
150	| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
151	| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
152	| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |
153	
154	### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage
155	
156	| ID | Name | Looks for |
157	|---|---|---|
158	| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
159	| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
160	| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
161	| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |
162	
163	## Using this well
164	
165	**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
166	category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.
167	
168	**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
169	or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
170	than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
171	enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
172	card is the claim.
173	
174	**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
175	on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
176	like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.
177	
178	**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
179	either attribution is fine — say which you chose.
180	
181	## What tools can and cannot contribute
182	
183	Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody
184	described in advance. That makes rules dependable about the shapes they know
185	and completely blind to everything else. Two consequences, and they point in
186	opposite directions:
187	
188	- **A rule firing has observed a pattern, not diagnosed a problem.** Every
189	  pattern in this taxonomy is the right thing to write somewhere, which is what
190	  each card's `Looks like it, but is not` section records.
191	  Some of what any rule reports is therefore wrong here, and saying which is
192	  part of the job.
193	- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
194	  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
195	  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
196	  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.
197	
198	Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
199	second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.
200
